body:
A meal on every corner

Walk through almost any big city in the world, and you will smell something delicious before you see it. That smell often comes from street food: simple, cheap meals cooked at a small stall or from a cart on wheels. In Thailand, Mexico, Turkey and dozens of other countries, millions of people eat their lunch this way every single day.

Why do people love it?

Street food is popular for three simple reasons: it is fast, it is cheap, and it is often extremely tasty. A cook can prepare a hot dish in front of you in just a few minutes, and you can watch every step, from the sizzling pan to the final touch. The aroma of grilled meat, fresh herbs or warm bread fills the air and pulls hungry customers closer.

A trip around the world in food

Every country has its own famous street snack. In Mexico, people enjoy soft tacos filled with meat, onion and lime. In Thailand, cooks fry noodles with prawns and egg in a dish called pad thai, which can be quite spicy. In Turkey, a sandwich called a döner is cut from meat that turns slowly on a large spit. These dishes are not fancy, but they tell you a great deal about the history and culture of a place.

More than just a snack

For many families, selling street food is also an important job. It helps them pay for their homes and send their children to school. Today, some famous chefs even say that the best cooking in a city is not always found in expensive restaurants — sometimes it is found on a busy street corner, cooked by someone who has made the same dish for thirty years. So next time you travel, try the food from a stall. It might become your favourite memory of the whole trip.

body:
Small insect, big job

Bees are tiny, but the work they do is enormous. A single hive can hold up to sixty thousand bees, and every one of them has a job. Some bees clean the hive, some guard the entrance, and others fly out to search for flowers. Without bees, many of the fruits and vegetables that we eat every day would simply disappear.

How bees talk to each other

Bees cannot speak, but they still share information in a clever way. When a worker bee finds a good flower, it flies back to the hive and performs a special dance. The direction and speed of the dance tell the other bees exactly where the flowers are and how far away they are. Scientists call this the "waggle dance", and it is one of the most amazing forms of animal communication ever discovered.

From flower to food

When a bee lands on a flower, tiny grains of pollen stick to its legs and body. As the bee moves from flower to flower, it carries the pollen with it, helping plants make seeds and fruit. This process is called pollination, and farmers depend on it for many of their crops, including apples, almonds and coffee. One bee alone cannot do very much, but millions of bees working together keep entire farms alive.

A hive with a queen

Inside every hive there is one very important bee: the queen. She does not collect pollen or build the hive; her only job is to lay eggs, sometimes more than a thousand a day. All the other bees protect her and feed her because the whole hive depends on her.

Why bees need our help

Sadly, the number of bees in the world is falling fast. Pollution, disease and the loss of wild flowers have made bees more endangered every year. Scientists warn that if bees disappear, our food supply could be in serious trouble. That is why more and more people are now planting flowers in their gardens just to give these small but powerful insects a place to live.

body:
A strange nightly show

Every night, while your body lies quiet and still, your mind can take you flying over mountains, walking through your old school, or talking to someone who lives far away. This is what happens when we dream. Almost everyone dreams while they are asleep, even if they do not always remember it in the morning.

What happens in the brain?

Scientists have studied sleep for many years, but they still do not fully understand why we dream. We know that during a stage of sleep called REM sleep, the brain becomes very active, almost as active as when we are awake. During this stage, the eyes move quickly under closed eyelids, and this is when the most detailed and colourful dreams usually happen.

Different ideas, different answers

One popular idea is that dreams help the brain sort out the events of the day, keeping useful memory and throwing away information we do not need. Another idea is that dreaming is simply a side effect of a busy brain, with no real purpose at all. A third idea suggests that dreams let us practise dealing with danger and difficult emotions in a safe way, using nothing but our own imagination.

When dreams turn scary

Not every dream is pleasant. A nightmare can wake a person up feeling frightened, with a fast heartbeat and sweaty hands. Nightmares often happen after a stressful day, after watching a scary film, or during a difficult time in someone's life. Most nightmares are completely harmless, even though they can feel very real while they last.

Still a mystery

Even with modern machines that can look inside the brain, every researcher agrees on one thing: dreaming is still one of the biggest mysteries of the human mind. Perhaps that is exactly what makes dreams so interesting. Tonight, when you close your eyes, remember that your brain is about to begin its own private film — and you are the only person who will ever see it.

body:
Before money existed

Long before coins and banknotes were invented, people still needed a way to get the things they did not have. A farmer with extra eggs might trade them for a fisherman's fish, and a fisherman might trade fish for warm clothes made by a weaver. This system worked, but it had one big problem: what happened if the weaver did not want any fish that day?

The first coins

To solve this problem, people slowly began using objects that almost everyone agreed had value, such as salt, shells or animal teeth. Around 2,700 years ago, in a place called Lydia, in what is now Turkey, people made the first metal coins. Coins were easy to carry, hard to copy, and everyone could agree on how much they were worth. This simple invention changed the way the whole world did business.

Paper, plastic and banks

Many centuries later, in China, merchants started using paper money instead of heavy bags of coins. Over time, buildings called banks appeared, where people could keep their money safely and borrow money when they needed it. In the twentieth century, small plastic cards arrived, allowing people to pay for things without carrying any cash at all.

Money without any coins

Today, many payments are completely cashless. People tap a card or a phone at a shop, and the money moves instantly from one bank account to another. Some countries are even experimenting with digital money that only exists on computers, with no physical coins or notes at all.

The real secret of money

Whether it is a shiny coin, a paper note, or a number on a screen, money only works because people trust it. If everybody suddenly stopped believing that money had value, the whole system would collapse overnight. In many ways, money is less about metal and paper, and more about the shared trust between millions of strangers.

body:
Not just in films

When you hear the word robot, you might imagine a metal character from a science-fiction film. But real robots are already all around us — in factories, hospitals, and even inside our homes — quietly doing jobs that used to take hours of human effort.

Working on the factory floor

Inside a modern factory, long metal arms lift heavy car parts, weld pieces of metal together, and paint vehicles with perfect, even lines. These robots can repeat the same task thousands of times a day without ever getting tired or making a mistake. Building a single vehicle once needed dozens of workers; today, robots can complete many of the same steps in a fraction of the time.

Helping doctors save lives

Robots are not only useful for heavy or repeated work. In some hospitals, surgeons now use robotic arms to perform delicate surgery. These robotic tools can move more precisely than a human hand, which allows the doctor to make smaller cuts, and this often helps patients recover faster.

Robots at home

At home, small robots can now vacuum the floor, cut the grass in the garden, or answer simple questions when you speak to them. None of these robots are as clever as the ones in movies, but they still save people a great deal of time every week.

Will robots take our jobs?

Many people worry that robots will completely replace human workers. It is true that robots have already changed some jobs, especially in factories. However, most experts believe that robots are better at repeating simple tasks, while humans are still much better at being creative, solving new problems, and caring for other people. The future, most scientists agree, is likely to be one where humans and robots work together, not against each other.

body:
A hotter planet

In the last few decades, scientists have measured something worrying: the average temperature of the Earth is slowly rising. This might not sound serious, but even a small change in temperature can affect oceans, forests and the weather that we experience every day.

Too much water, or not enough

One clear result of a warming planet is more extreme weather. In some regions, heavy rain now causes serious floods, pushing water into streets and homes within hours. In other regions, the opposite happens: a long drought dries up rivers and makes it very difficult for farmers to grow food. The same warming planet can create these two very different, and equally dangerous, problems.

Stronger storms

Warmer oceans also give more energy to storms. Hurricanes and typhoons that form over warm water can grow bigger and stronger than they did in the past, bringing dangerous winds and huge waves to coastal cities. Weather experts now warn people earlier, but strong storms can still cause enormous damage in just a few hours.

Why is the climate changing?

Most scientists agree that the main cause of these changes is human activity, especially burning coal, oil and gas for energy. This releases gases into the air that trap heat, slowly changing the climate of the whole planet, not just one country.

What can be done?

The good news is that people can act. Governments are building more wind farms and solar panels, cities are planting more trees, and many families are trying to reduce the amount of energy they use every day. No single action will solve the problem alone, but scientists say that millions of small changes, made together, can still make a real difference.

body:
Movies before words

Before actors could speak on screen, cinemas were full of silent films. For almost thirty years, from the 1890s until the late 1920s, every movie in the world was silent, and audiences still filled theatres night after night.

How could a movie be silent?

Without recorded sound, filmmakers had to be extremely creative. Actors used big, clear body movements and dramatic facial expressions so the audience could understand the story without hearing a single word. In the cinema itself, a pianist or a small band played live music next to the screen, adding excitement to chase scenes and sadness to emotional moments.

The kings and queens of comedy

Some of the biggest stars of this era were comedians. Charlie Chaplin, dressed as a clumsy but kind character called the Tramp, made millions of people laugh using nothing but movement and timing. Buster Keaton became famous for performing incredibly dangerous stunts himself, never once smiling on camera, which somehow made his films even funnier.

A remarkable invention

Making moving pictures at all was seen as a remarkable invention at the time; many early audiences had never seen anything like it and were amazed simply by images that moved. As cameras and film technology slowly improved, directors learned new tricks, using close-ups, fast cuts and clever lighting to tell more and more exciting stories.

The end of an era

In 1927, a film called "The Jazz Singer" surprised audiences with a few moments of recorded speech, and within just a few years, almost every studio was making "talkies" instead. Silent films quickly disappeared from cinemas, but many of their stars became legends who are still studied and admired by filmmakers today.

body:
Shopping without leaving home

Thirty years ago, buying a new pair of shoes or a book meant travelling to a shop, choosing an item from a shelf, and paying at a till. Today, millions of people complete the same purchase from their sofa, using nothing but a phone or a laptop.

The rise of online shopping

Large online platforms now sell almost anything imaginable, from fresh vegetables to furniture, cars and even houses. A shopper can compare prices from different retailers in seconds, something that used to take an entire afternoon of walking between different shops.

Trusting a stranger's opinion

Since online shoppers cannot touch or try a product before buying it, they often rely on a customer review instead. Reading what hundreds of other buyers thought about a product's quality helps people feel more confident before clicking the "buy" button, even though they have never met any of those reviewers.

From click to doorstep

Once an order is placed, the real journey begins. Warehouses use fast machines to find and pack items, and companies compete to offer the quickest delivery, sometimes bringing a package to your door on the very same day it was ordered. This speed would have seemed almost impossible a generation ago.

Staying safe online

Of course, shopping online also brings new worries, especially about money and personal information. Trustworthy websites use a secure connection to protect card details, shown by a small padlock symbol in the browser. Experts still advise shoppers to be careful, check reviews, and only buy from websites they trust, because not every online shop is honest.

body:
A world full of celebration

No matter where you travel, you will almost always find people preparing to celebrate something. Festivals bring communities together, filling streets with music, colour, and the smell of special food, even when the reasons for the celebration are completely different from one culture to another.

Lights, colour and fire

In India, during the festival of Diwali, millions of small lamps and bright fireworks light up the night sky to celebrate the victory of light over darkness. In Spain, the town of Valencia holds a huge festival called Las Fallas, where enormous, colourful statues are built and then dramatically burned in the street.

Dressing up for the occasion

Many festivals also involve wearing a special costume. During Carnival in Brazil, dancers wear extremely bright, feathered outfits and perform in huge parades that last for days. In Venice, Italy, people wear elegant masks during their famous Carnival, hiding their identity while they enjoy the celebrations.

Remembering the past

Not every festival is only about fun; some are about remembering. In Mexico, during the Day of the Dead, families build colourful altars covered in flowers and photographs to honour an ancestor who has died. Instead of being sad, families remember these relatives with music, stories, and a shared feast of their loved one's favourite food.

Why festivals matter

Every festival follows its own tradition, passed down from parents to children for many generations. Even though the customs are different everywhere, festivals always seem to do the same important job: they bring people together, strengthen communities, and give everyone, for at least one day, a good reason to smile.

body:
More than just a sound

A short burst of laughter might seem like a small, simple thing, but scientists who study it have discovered something surprising: laughing changes what happens inside your entire body, from your brain to your heart.

What happens when we laugh?

When something makes you laugh, your brain quickly releases special chemicals, including a hormone that reduces pain and improves your mood almost immediately. At the same time, laughing exercises your chest and stomach muscles, and it can even lower your blood pressure for a short time afterwards.

A natural instinct

Interestingly, laughing appears to be an instinct, not something we learn from watching others. Babies who were born completely deaf, and who have never heard another person laugh, still laugh in exactly the same way as everyone else. This suggests that laughter is written into human biology from the very beginning of life.

Why we rarely laugh alone

Researchers have also found that laughter is deeply social. People are around thirty times more likely to laugh when they are with other people than when they are completely alone, even while watching the exact same funny video. This might explain why comedy shows feel funnier in a full cinema than they do at home by yourself.

Good medicine for the body

Doctors now believe that regular laughter can even help protect the immune system, making it a little easier for the body to fight off illness. Laughing also reduces stress, helping people feel calmer after a difficult day. So the next time you share a joke with a friend, remember: you are not just having fun, you are doing something genuinely good for your health.

body:
The Morales family

Every family has many different personalities, and the Morales family is no exception. Let's meet them and find out what they are like.

Grandma Rosa and Dad

Grandma Rosa is extremely affectionate: she hugs everybody who walks into her kitchen. She is also honest, so she always tells you the truth, even when you do not want to hear it. Best of all, she is patient and never loses her temper. Her son Carlos is completely different. He is ambitious and wants to become the manager of his company before he is forty. He is very competitive too: he hates losing, even in a simple family card game! At home he can be bossy and tells everybody what to do.

Mum and Uncle Marco

Carlos's wife, Elena, is the calm centre of the family. She is sensible, so she makes good decisions, and she is reliable: if she says she will do something, she does it. She is self-confident as well, so she is never afraid to speak in a meeting. Uncle Marco is the most sociable person in the house. He loves parties and meeting new people. He is also charming, and everybody likes him within five minutes.

The teenagers

Lucas, who is sixteen, is a typical teenager. He is rebellious and hates rules. He is independent and wants to do everything on his own. He is also moody, happy at breakfast and silent at dinner, and very stubborn, so arguing with him is useless. His cousin Ana is only fourteen, but she is very mature for her age and talks like an adult. She is sensitive, which means that small comments can hurt her feelings, and sometimes she feels insecure about herself. Before every exam she becomes anxious and cannot sleep.

The youngest

Finally, there is six-year-old Sofia. Everybody gives her everything she wants, so she has become spoilt. She can also be selfish, and she never shares her sweets. But Sofia is very imaginative too. She invents wonderful stories about talking animals and magic forests, and the whole family loves to listen.

Is anybody perfect?

Nobody in the Morales family is perfect, and that is what makes them interesting. Every personality has good and difficult sides. Learning the right adjectives helps us to describe other people, and ourselves, more accurately.

notes: un- , in- , dis- are common negative prefixes: honest → dishonest , reliable → unreliable . in- changes to im- before b, m, p ( patient → impatient ), to ir- before r, and to il- before l.
